presented_options.A: 0 = OK, 1 = SQL error, 2 = CLI usage error, 3 = storage/IO error
presented_options.B: 0 = OK, 1 = any error (SQL, CLI, or IO collapsed together), with stderr distinguishing the category
presented_options.D: 0 = OK, 1 = SQL error, 2 = storage/IO, 3 = CLI usage (CLI last because it's the rarest)

answers.rationale: CLI usage errors (missing args, bad format) exit with code 2, but all errors from cli.run() — which covers SQL, IO, storage — exit with code 1 (main.rs:130-136). Within batch execution, all failure categories are collapsed to exit code 1, with stderr distinguishing the category via MiniDbError::Display.

presented_options.A: each statement is implicitly wrapped in its own transaction that commits on success, matching BEGIN/COMMIT semantics
presented_options.B: statements run without any transaction; durability is deferred to a periodic checkpoint
presented_options.C: statements run under a long-running implicit transaction that commits only when the process exits
presented_options.D: statements inherit the transaction of the previous BEGIN if any was ever opened in the session

answers.rationale: TransactionManager::auto_begin() starts a new transaction if auto_commit is true (txn.rs:86-94), and auto_commit() commits it after the statement (txn.rs:96-101). The CLI calls auto_begin before execution and auto_commit after (cli.rs:397-419), giving each statement its own implicit transaction matching BEGIN/COMMIT semantics.

presented_options.A: ARIES-style WAL with explicit undo and redo records plus a separate dirty-page table checkpoint
presented_options.B: synchronous double-write: every page is written to a scratch region before being written to its home location
presented_options.C: an append-only write-ahead log, replayed at startup to re-apply committed transactions and drop the uncommitted suffix
presented_options.D: shadow paging: mutations go to a copy page; a pointer swap at commit promotes the copy atomically

answers.rationale: The WAL is an append-only log (write_record appends and fsyncs). On startup, wal.replay() reads all records and cli.rs:replay_wal() replays committed transactions, dropping uncommitted ones (cli.rs:76-130). The WAL is then cleared.

presented_options.A: records are padded to a fixed 512-byte sector boundary; partial sectors are discarded
presented_options.B: no per-record check; a single CRC covers the whole WAL file on clean shutdown
presented_options.C: records are written in pairs (main + mirror); replay prefers whichever pair verifies
presented_options.D: each record carries a CRC32; replay stops at the first record whose CRC fails to verify

answers.rationale: Each WAL record is written with a CRC32 (wal.rs:207-220). During replay, each record's CRC is verified; on mismatch, replay stops and discards the rest of the WAL (wal.rs:257-259).

presented_options.A: materialising execution: each operator fully computes its output set before the next operator starts reading
presented_options.B: push-based execution where operators drive their children forward via a single dataflow scheduler
presented_options.C: vectorised/columnar execution where each operator produces and consumes batches of column vectors
presented_options.D: a Volcano-style iterator tree: each operator exposes open/next/close and returns one row (or tiny batch) at a time

answers.rationale: The executor is materializing: each operator (SeqScan, Filter, Project, Sort, etc.) fully computes its output into an ExecutionResult with all rows before the next operator processes it (exec/mod.rs:232-459). There is no iterator/volcano open/next/close pattern.

presented_options.A: a B-tree keyed by the composite (index_key, row_id); duplicates are naturally ordered by row_id
presented_options.B: an inverted list built lazily on first query and cached in memory
presented_options.C: a hash map keyed by the indexed value alone; collisions chain a Vec<RowId>
presented_options.D: a bitmap per distinct value; looked up with bitwise AND for compound predicates

answers.rationale: The index is implemented as BTreeMap<IndexKey, Vec<RowId>> (btree.rs:11). Each unique indexed value maps to a Vec<RowId> of matching rows. While backed by a BTreeMap (not HashMap), the logical organization matches: keyed by indexed value, with row IDs chained per value.

presented_options.A: IndexScan and SeqScan as two variants of a single ScanKind enum so the executor only has one Scan operator
presented_options.B: Filter and Project exist as separate types rather than being fused into one 'SelectExpr' operator
presented_options.C: SeqScan, IndexScan, Filter, Project, NestedLoopJoin, Sort, Limit, Insert, Update, Delete each as a distinct type
presented_options.D: Update and Delete are distinct operators rather than one 'Mutate' operator parameterised by a kind

answers.rationale: SeqScan and IndexScan are separate variants of PhysicalPlan, not unified via a ScanKind enum. Option A describes a ScanKind enum pattern that does not exist in this codebase. Options B, C, and D all accurately describe what IS present.

presented_options.A: inside the storage layer, which transparently redirects SeqScan calls through the index when available
presented_options.B: inside the parser, encoded as a special AST node when the WHERE clause mentions an indexed column
presented_options.C: inside the planner when lowering the logical plan to a physical plan; the parser only produces ASTs
presented_options.D: inside the executor at open() time, after consulting the catalog to see whether an index is applicable

answers.rationale: Index selection happens in LogicalPlan::plan_select (logical.rs:83-109) and try_extract_index_predicate (logical.rs:166-228), which is part of the planner lowering the logical plan. The parser only produces ASTs; the planner makes the physical scan choice.

presented_options.A: errors are encoded as strings (Result<T, String>) so every caller formats them uniformly
presented_options.B: each subsystem defines its own error type; the CLI sees a Box<dyn Error> and pattern-matches on downcast
presented_options.C: errors are propagated via panics with typed payloads and caught at the CLI via std::panic::catch_unwind
presented_options.D: a single crate-wide error enum with one variant per source is the return type of top-level entry points; lower modules convert at their public boundary

answers.rationale: MiniDbError is a single crate-wide enum with variants per source: Parse, Syntax, TypeMismatch, TypeError, Runtime, Storage, Io, Transaction, Constraint, NotFound, Serialization (error.rs:4-16). It is the return type of top-level entry points via the Result<T> alias.

presented_options.A: table / csv / json selectable via a --format CLI flag or a .format meta-command in the REPL
presented_options.B: table / json / messagepack selectable only via an environment variable MINIDB_FORMAT
presented_options.C: table output only; downstream callers are expected to parse and re-format it themselves
presented_options.D: the format is fixed at build time via a Cargo feature (--features=json)

answers.rationale: Output formats Table, Csv, Json are selectable via --format CLI flag (main.rs:90-105) or .format meta-command in the REPL (cli.rs:269-276). The format_table, format_csv, and format_json methods are implemented in exec/mod.rs.

presented_options.A: when --format json is active, the JSON value is the only thing on stdout — no banner lines, no trailing 'ok' line
presented_options.B: --quiet suppresses the per-statement summary entirely; stdout still carries the data stream
presented_options.C: per-statement summary lines (e.g. `ok 3 rows`) go to stderr, letting callers pipe stdout straight into another tool
presented_options.D: the per-statement summary is written to stdout immediately before the data so callers see it arrive first

answers.rationale: Per-statement summaries go to stderr via eprintln! (cli.rs:297, 304, 311, 335, 343, 379, 387, 409, 415), not stdout. Option D claims they go to stdout immediately before the data, which is inconsistent with the codebase.

presented_options.A: pages are a mixed size; the header chooses between 4 KiB and 16 KiB per table based on row width
presented_options.B: pages are identified by a newtype over u64 (PageId) rather than a bare integer
presented_options.C: the page size is a single compile-time constant referenced throughout storage
presented_options.D: the heap stores rows inside fixed-size pages rather than one file per row

answers.rationale: PAGE_SIZE is a single compile-time constant of 4096 (storage/mod.rs:8). There is no mixed-size page scheme. PageId is a newtype over u64 (mod.rs:11). Pages are fixed-size. Option A's claim of mixed sizes is inconsistent.

presented_options.A: all three rows — every fsynced WAL record is replayed on startup
presented_options.B: the two earliest rows — only WAL records that survive the CRC check are replayed; the trailing one is dropped
presented_options.C: no rows — a transaction whose WAL trail has no COMMIT record is treated as an uncommitted prefix and discarded
presented_options.D: an error at startup demanding manual recovery before any SELECT can run

answers.rationale: Recovery in cli.rs:76-130 collects committed_txns from Commit records. Only records whose tx_id is in committed_txns are applied. Without a COMMIT record, the transaction is treated as uncommitted and all its WAL records are discarded. The SELECT sees no rows.
